Cannabis 101

Edible Myths, Busted: Onset, Dosing, Taste and Safety

Edibles have a reputation, and not all of it is earned. Here are seven common myths, what's actually true and how to enjoy edibles with confidence.

By the High Society teamPublished October 24, 20266 min read

06min readCannabis 101
In this article
  1. Myth 1: An edible kicks in within minutes
  2. Myth 2: Any edible will flatten you
  3. Myth 3: Dosing edibles is guesswork
  4. Myth 4: Edibles always taste like cannabis
  5. Myth 5: You need years of experience to try edibles
  6. Myth 6: Edibles are dangerous
  7. Myth 7: One edible is like any other
  8. Edible myths, wrapped up: enjoying edibles with confidence
  9. Frequently asked questions

Key takeaways

  • An edible may not kick in for 2 hours and can take up to 4 hours to reach full effect, so wait before taking more.
  • The dose decides the experience, and Michigan caps adult-use edibles at 10 mg of THC per serving.
  • Canadian public health officials suggest a first dose of no more than 2.5 mg of THC.
  • A fatal cannabis-only overdose is unlikely, but too much is miserable, and kids can get seriously ill.
  • Keep edibles in their original child-resistant packaging, locked away from kids and pets.

Edible myths spread fast, and a few of them lead to rough nights. The truth is more useful: edibles take longer to start than smoking, the dose on the label shapes the experience, and the real risks are manageable once you know them. Here are seven myths, what research and Michigan's rules actually say, and how to enjoy edibles with confidence.

Myth 1: An edible kicks in within minutes

Swallowed THC has a longer trip to make. It's absorbed through the gut and processed by the liver, so edibles start slowly. The CDC notes you may not feel an edible for as long as 2 hours. Canada's chief medical officers of health add that the full effect can take up to 4. In one small controlled study, effects from THC brownies peaked 1.5 to 3 hours after eating and lasted 6 to 8 hours.

That delay causes a lot of edible trouble, because people take a second dose when the first one seems not to be working. Michigan labels list an activation time, so check it, note when you ate and wait at least 2 hours before deciding on more. Our guide to edibles covers the basics.

Myth 2: Any edible will flatten you

The dose decides. In that same brownie study, effects generally rose with the dose. A small edible can be mild, and a large one overwhelming, especially without tolerance.

Michigan caps adult-use edibles at 10 mg of THC per serving and 200 mg per package, so one labeled serving is a ceiling, not a target.

Myth 3: Dosing edibles is guesswork

Labels take most of the guessing out. Every Michigan package lists its THC and CBD content, with a note that actual values may vary by 10%, so you can do simple math:

  • A 10 mg gummy cut into quarters gives you about 2.5 mg per piece.
  • A 100 mg chocolate bar with 10 squares holds 10 mg per square.

Canada's chief medical officers of health suggest no more than 2.5 mg of THC to start, for anything you eat or drink. Our THC dosage guide walks through the numbers, and our budtenders can help you read a label in store.

Myth 4: Edibles always taste like cannabis

Some do, especially homemade or whole-plant infusions with an herbal, grassy note. Many gummies, chocolates and drinks are flavored so the cannabis barely comes through. That's also why edibles can be mistaken for ordinary snacks. It's one reason Michigan bans edibles shaped like people, animals or fruit and keeps the word candy off packaging. Our guide to choosing THC gummies covers flavors and formats.

Myth 5: You need years of experience to try edibles

Edibles can suit beginners, as long as you go low and slow. Pick a low-dose product or split a piece. Settle in somewhere comfortable with nowhere to drive, skip the alcohol and give it a full 2 hours. If you're pregnant, breastfeeding, taking medications or managing a health condition, talk with a clinician before trying edibles.

Myth 6: Edibles are dangerous

The truth has two sides. The CDC says a fatal overdose caused only by cannabis is unlikely, but cannabis isn't harmless. Taking too much can mean an intensely uncomfortable few hours and a higher risk of injuries such as falls or crashes.

Children face the biggest risk. A study of U.S. poison center data found that reported edible exposures in children under 6 rose from 207 in 2017 to 3,054 in 2021. Nearly all happened at home, and about 23% of the children were admitted to the hospital. The CDC notes that young children who eat cannabis are more likely to need hospital care than older kids.

Keep edibles in their original child-resistant packaging, in a locked box, away from kids and pets. If a child eats one, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222, or 911 in an emergency. If a pet does, call your veterinarian. Our pet safety guide covers animals, and our tips for getting unhigh help if you took too much.

Myth 7: One edible is like any other

Edibles differ more than people expect:

TypeWhat to know
Gummies and chocolatesEasy to portion; check the mg per piece
Baked goodsHarder to split evenly; homemade batches vary most
DrinksMichigan caps adult-use drinks at 10 mg per serving and 100 mg per container
Capsules and tincturesWhatever you swallow acts like an edible
Fast-acting productsMade to start sooner, but timing still varies by person

Medical edibles for registered patients can hold up to 50 mg of THC per dose, five times an adult-use serving. Check which kind you have before you eat it.

Edible myths, wrapped up: enjoying edibles with confidence

  • Begin at 2.5 mg of THC or less, and wait at least 2 hours.
  • Read the label for mg per serving and the activation time.
  • Store edibles locked, in their original packaging, away from kids and pets.
  • Keep the Poison Control number handy: 1-800-222-1222.
  • Don't drive while effects last, which can be 4 to 12 hours or longer.

21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

Frequently asked questions

Why haven't I felt my edible yet?

Because THC you swallow has to pass through your gut and liver first. You may not feel an edible for as long as 2 hours, and its full effect can take up to 4. Edibles can also feel stronger and less predictable than inhaled cannabis. Give it at least 2 hours before you think about taking more.

Can you overdose on edibles?

A fatal overdose from cannabis alone is unlikely, according to the CDC, but taking too much is a real risk. It can bring several intensely uncomfortable hours and a higher chance of falls or other injuries. Children are at greater risk: young kids who eat cannabis are more likely to need hospital care than older children.

What should I do if a child eats an edible?

Call Poison Control right away at 1-800-222-1222, and call 911 if the child is hard to wake, has trouble breathing or has a seizure. Keep the package so you can say what was eaten and how much. Then store the rest in its original child-resistant packaging, locked and out of reach.

Are fast-acting edibles different?

They're made to start sooner, but timing still varies from person to person. Handle a fast-acting product like any edible: start with a low dose, check the label's activation time and give it plenty of time before having more.

Sources

  1. CDC: Cannabis frequently asked questionscdc.gov
  2. Council of Chief Medical Officers of Health (Canada): statement on cannabis extracts, edibles and topicals, 2020canada.ca
  3. Vandrey et al. (2017), pharmacokinetic profile of oral cannabis in humans, Journal of Analytical Toxicologypmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  4. Tweet et al. (2023), pediatric edible cannabis exposures and acute toxicity, 2017-2021, Pediatricspubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
  5. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: Marihuana Rules, R 420.1 to R 420.1004, including edible packaging and labeling (PDF)michigan.gov
  6. Michigan Cannabis Regulatory Agency: technical bulletin on maximum THC in infused products, April 2025 (PDF)michigan.gov
21+

For adults 21 and older. Keep cannabis away from children and pets, and never drive after consuming. Michigan law does not allow cannabis use in public places.
